wiki-gondwana.title: Gondwana (Wikipedia)
wiki-gondwana.author: Wikipedia contributors
wiki-gondwana.kind: encyclopedia (secondary, used as a pointer to the works it cites)
wiki-gondwana.rights: CC BY-SA 4.0 text; facts cited only, no text reused.
wiki-gondwana.checked: Opened 27 Oct 2026. Assembly c. 800 to 650 Ma (East African Orogeny) to c. 600 to 530 Ma (Brasiliano and Kuunga orogenies); remnants include South America, Africa, Antarctica, Australia, Zealandia, Arabia and India; Pangaea's break-up began with the Central Atlantic magmatic province, peaking c. 200 Ma; Africa and Antarctica began to part c. 180 to 160 Ma; South Atlantic rifting propagated north c. 150 or 140 Ma, spreading c. 135 to 130 Ma, rifting north of the equator after 120.4 Ma until c. 100 to 96 Ma; footprints suggest a land link as late as the early Aptian (c. 120 Ma); 'considerable debate over the exact timing'.

wiki-benue-trough.title: Benue Trough (Wikipedia)
wiki-benue-trough.author: Wikipedia contributors
wiki-benue-trough.kind: encyclopedia (secondary, used as a pointer to the works it cites)
wiki-benue-trough.rights: CC BY-SA 4.0 text; facts cited only, no text reused.
wiki-benue-trough.checked: Opened 27 Oct 2026. About 1,000 km north-east from the Bight of Benin to Lake Chad, about 150 km wide, its southern limit the northern edge of the Niger Delta; rifting began at the start of the Cretaceous (145 Ma); intense compression and folding in the Santonian, about 84 Ma; commonly explained as an aulacogen, the inactive arm of a three-armed rift as South America separated from Africa; coal swamps in the Anambra Basin; the Enugu deposits formed in brackish marshes in the Late Campanian to early Maastrichtian, around 70 Ma. No specific date for the start of rifting beyond 'the start of the Cretaceous' (the outline's 118 Ma is not supported).

usgs-niger-delta.title: Tertiary Niger Delta (Akata-Agbada) Petroleum System, Niger Delta Province (Open-File Report 99-50-H, chapter A)

usgs-niger-delta.rights: US government work, public domain; facts cited.

It does not say that people moved south towards the Niger or Lake Chad.

kuper-kropelin-2006.title: Climate-Controlled Holocene Occupation in the Sahara: Motor of Africa's Evolution
kuper-kropelin-2006.author: Rudolph Kuper and Stefan Kröpelin, Science 313, 803-807
kuper-kropelin-2006.rights: Cited and described; no text or figures reused.
kuper-kropelin-2006.checked: Opened 27 Oct 2026 (author copy at the University of Cologne). About the eastern Sahara (Egypt, Sudan and adjacent Libya and Chad): humid from 8500 to 5300 BCE; regular rains stopped reaching the Egyptian Sahara by 5300 BCE and full desert returned about 3500 BCE; people moved to the Nile valley and ecological refuges, and towards today's Sahel and the Sudanese plains. The authors suggest the process applied to the whole Sahara, an inference rather than a finding for the central and western Sahara.
